subject: Science
title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
summary: A current-carrying wire behaves like a magnet, a magnet pushes on a current-carrying wire, and both facts run the safety wiring of your house. The rationalised chapter is short (motor, induction and generator were removed), which makes the four topics that remain, field lines, field of a straight wire, loop and solenoid, Fleming's left-hand rule and domestic circuits, very predictable in the board paper.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 10 Science is one 80-mark theory paper covering physics, chemistry and biology. This chapter belongs to Unit IV, Effects of Current (Chapters 11 and 12), which carries 13 marks together. Magnetic Effects alone typically fetches 4 to 6 marks: one or two 1-mark items (an MCQ on solenoid or field lines, or an Assertion–Reason), and one 2-mark or 3-mark question, with a diagram (solenoid field, straight-wire field, Fleming's left-hand rule or the domestic circuit) asked most years. A 5-mark question combining Fleming's rule with domestic circuits appears every few years.

question_types.note: Shape of the field around a straight wire (concentric circles); field inside a long solenoid (uniform, same at all points); direction of field above or below an east-west wire; direction of force on an electron or proton entering a field; what changes for a charged particle moving in a field; current at the time of a short circuit; colour of the earth wire; which wire the fuse is put in.

Field lines never intersect (reason: the compass would have two directions); field lines are closed curves; solenoid field is uniform inside; force is largest when current is perpendicular to the field; fuse must be in the live wire; earthing protects against shock.

Two properties of field lines; right-hand thumb rule with the east-west wire example; why the field of a solenoid resembles a bar magnet; what an electromagnet is and one use; how the field of a straight wire changes with current and distance; what a short circuit is; why an appliance is earthed; meaning of 50 Hz.

Describe the activity showing concentric field lines around a straight conductor; draw the solenoid field and list two ways it differs from a bar magnet's; state Fleming's left-hand rule and apply it to a given direction of current and field; force on a charge at rest, moving parallel and moving perpendicular to a field; the 2 kW oven on a 5 A circuit; short circuit versus overloading with one precaution each.

Fleming's left-hand rule with the aluminium-rod activity plus factors affecting the force; solenoid field, electromagnet and its uses; the domestic circuit schematic with live, neutral, earth, main fuse, meter and distribution to 15 A and 5 A circuits, followed by functions of fuse and earth wire; sometimes combined with the AC supply characteristics (220 V, 50 Hz).

A passage on an electromagnet or solenoid (poles, uniform field, factors increasing strength), or on a household wiring fault (fuse rating, overloading calculation, earthing), followed by four sub-questions of which one is usually a small calculation such as I = P/V.

hot_topics: Magnetic field lines of a bar magnet and their four properties (never intersect, closed curves, N to S outside, closer means stronger)
Field around a straight conductor: concentric circles, right-hand thumb rule, dependence on current and distance
Solenoid: field pattern, uniform field inside, comparison with a bar magnet, electromagnet
Fleming's left-hand rule and the aluminium-rod activity; when the force is largest
Direction questions: electron beam, alpha particle, proton in a field (velocity and momentum change, speed does not)
Domestic electric circuit: live, neutral, earth wires, main fuse, 15 A and 5 A circuits, parallel connection
Short circuit versus overloading, fuse rating and the 2 kW oven on a 5 A line
AC supply at home: 220 V, 50 Hz, reversal 100 times a second

sections.heading: Introduction: Oersted's experiment (Activity 12.1)
sections.body:
The previous chapter dealt with the heating effect of current. This chapter starts from a second effect that Hans Christian Oersted stumbled on in 1820: a compass needle placed near a wire swings the moment current flows through the wire. Nothing touches the needle. The current has produced a magnetic field in the space around the wire, and the compass, being a tiny bar magnet, turns to line up with that field. Oersted's observation was the first proof that electricity and magnetism are two faces of one phenomenon, and it opened up the whole subject of electromagnetism.

Activity 12.1 is the version the examiner expects you to describe. A thick straight copper wire XY is connected in a circuit with a battery, a plug key and a resistor. A small compass is placed horizontally near the wire. When the key is inserted, the needle deflects. If you reverse the battery connections so that the current flows the other way, the needle deflects the other way. Two conclusions come straight from this: a current produces a magnetic field, and the direction of that field depends on the direction of the current.

Keep in mind the two ways the chapter will now build on this. First, we study what the field of a current looks like for different shapes of conductor (straight wire, circular loop, solenoid). Second, we turn the idea around: if a current makes a magnet feel a force, then by Newton's third law a magnet must make a current-carrying wire feel a force too. That is Section 12.3, and it leads to Fleming's left-hand rule.
sections.tip: When asked why the compass deflects, do not say 'because of the current'. Say: the current produces a magnetic field around the wire, and the compass needle, being a small magnet, experiences a force in that field and turns.

sections.heading: 12.1 Magnetic Field and Field Lines
sections.body:
A compass needle is a small bar magnet. The end that points north is its north-seeking pole, or north pole; the other end is the south pole. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. When a compass is brought near a bar magnet, the needle deflects because the magnet exerts a force on the needle's poles.

The region around a magnet in which its force can be detected is called its magnetic field. Activity 12.2 makes the field visible: place a bar magnet on a sheet of paper, sprinkle iron filings around it and tap the board. Every filing becomes a tiny magnet in the field and settles along a curve. The curves are the magnetic field lines. Activity 12.3 draws one such line properly: put a compass near the north pole of the magnet, mark the two ends of the needle, move the compass so its south pole sits where its north pole was, and keep going until you reach the south pole of the magnet. Joining the dots gives one field line; repeating gives the full pattern.

Magnetic field is a quantity with both magnitude and direction. By convention the direction of the field at a point is the direction in which the north pole of a compass needle placed there would move. The board wants these properties of field lines written as separate points:

  1. Outside the magnet the field lines emerge from the north pole and merge into the south pole; inside the magnet they run from south pole to north pole. So field lines are closed curves.
  2. Where the lines are crowded (near the poles) the field is strong; where they are far apart the field is weak. The deflection of a compass increases as you move it towards a pole.
  3. No two field lines ever cross. If they did, a compass at the crossing point would have to point in two directions at once, which is impossible.
  4. The tangent at any point on a field line gives the direction of the field at that point.

A uniform magnetic field is one that has the same magnitude and direction at every point in a region. It is drawn as equally spaced parallel straight lines with arrows all pointing the same way. This drawing is an NCERT in-text question and a frequent 1-mark item.
sections.tip: The 'why do field lines not intersect' answer is a marking point on its own: at the point of intersection there would be two directions of the field, so a compass needle would point two ways at once, which is not possible.

sections.heading: 12.2 Magnetic Field due to a Current-carrying Conductor (Activity 12.4)
sections.body:
Activity 12.1 showed that a current produces a field. Activity 12.4 finds its direction. Connect a long straight copper wire in series with two or three cells and a plug key. Lay the wire parallel to and directly above a compass needle, pointing north-south. When current flows from north to south through the wire, the north pole of the needle moves towards the east. Now interchange the cell connections so that the current flows from south to north: the needle now swings towards the west.

The examiner's takeaway is the pairing of observation and conclusion. Observation: the needle deflects when current flows. Conclusion: a current-carrying conductor has a magnetic field around it. Observation: reversing the current reverses the deflection. Conclusion: the direction of the magnetic field depends on the direction of the current.

A common lab-based MCQ describes a student who reports that (i) the deflection of the compass reverses when the terminals of the battery are interchanged, and (ii) the deflection decreases when the compass is moved farther from the wire. Both are correct reports. A student who claims the deflection stays unchanged on reversing the current has made a wrong observation; that is the option to reject.

What determines the actual pattern of the field, that is, how the field lines are arranged in space? The pattern depends on the shape of the conductor. The chapter therefore takes three shapes one by one: a straight wire (12.2.1), a circular loop (12.2.3) and a solenoid (12.2.4). Whatever the shape, two facts stay true throughout: the field at a point grows if the current grows, and the field at a point falls as you move away from the wire.

formulas.expr: B ∝ I (at a fixed point near the conductor)
where: magnetic field strength at the point

sections.tip: In Activity 12.4 the wire must be kept parallel to the needle, that is, along north-south, before the current is switched on. If the wire is at right angles to the needle the needle is already along the field of the wire and hardly deflects.

sections.heading: 12.2.1 Magnetic Field due to a Current through a Straight Conductor (Activity 12.5)
sections.body:
This activity is asked as a 3-mark 'describe an activity' question and the marking scheme rewards the set-up, the observation and the two variations. Pass a long thick copper wire vertically through the centre of a horizontal cardboard sheet. Connect it in series with a 12 V battery, a rheostat, an ammeter (0 to 5 A) and a plug key. Sprinkle iron filings uniformly on the cardboard, close the key so that current flows, and tap the cardboard gently.

Observation: the filings arrange themselves in concentric circles centred on the wire. These circles are the magnetic field lines of a straight current-carrying conductor. To find their direction, place a compass at a point P on one circle; the north pole of the needle points along the field. Reversing the current reverses the direction of the needle, so the direction of the field lines reverses when the current reverses.

Variation 1, change the current: use the rheostat to increase the current, keeping the compass at the same point. The deflection increases. So the magnitude of the field at a given point increases as the current through the wire increases.

Variation 2, change the distance: keep the current fixed and move the compass from P to a farther point Q. The deflection decreases. So the field produced by a given current decreases as the distance from the wire increases. You can see this in the pattern too: the concentric circles get larger and farther apart as you move out from the wire.

Two sentences to memorise for the 2-mark version: the magnetic field at a point due to a straight current-carrying conductor is directly proportional to the current and inversely proportional to the distance of the point from the conductor.

where: perpendicular distance of the point from the wire

sections.tip: Draw the wire vertical, the cardboard horizontal, three or four circles centred on the wire, an arrow on each circle, and a compass on one circle. A diagram without arrows loses the 'direction' mark.

sections.heading: 12.2.2 Right-Hand Thumb Rule
sections.body:
The right-hand thumb rule gives the direction of the field around a straight current-carrying conductor. Imagine holding the conductor in your right hand so that the thumb points in the direction of the current. The curled fingers then wrap around the conductor in the direction of the magnetic field lines. The same rule is also called Maxwell's corkscrew rule: if you drive a corkscrew forward in the direction of the current, the direction in which you turn the handle is the direction of the field.

The way to apply it in the exam is Example 12.1. A horizontal power line carries current from east to west. What is the field at a point directly below and directly above it? Point the right thumb towards the west. The fingers curl so that, viewed from the east end of the wire (looking along the current), the field goes clockwise in a plane perpendicular to the wire, and anticlockwise when viewed from the west end. Working through the curl: directly below the wire the field points towards the south, and directly above the wire it points towards the north. If you want to check, imagine your thumb pointing west and your palm facing down: the fingertips below the wire point south and the knuckles above point north.

A second favourite: a vertical wire carries current from top to bottom. Viewed from above, the field goes clockwise (thumb pointing down and away from you, fingers curl clockwise as seen from above). If the current flows upward, the field is anticlockwise as seen from above. Questions often reverse this: 'to produce a clockwise field seen from above, current must flow from top to bottom'.

The rule works for any small piece of a bent wire as well, which is how the chapter gets the field of a loop and a solenoid in the next two subsections.
sections.tip: Do not confuse this rule with Fleming's left-hand rule. Right-hand thumb rule: one thumb, one set of curled fingers, gives the field of a current. Fleming's left hand: three fingers at right angles, gives the force on a current in a given field.

sections.heading: 12.2.3 Magnetic Field due to a Current through a Circular Loop (Activity 12.6)
sections.body:
Bend the straight wire into a circular loop and pass a current through it. Near the wire, at every point on the loop, the field lines are still small concentric circles. As you move away from the wire the circles grow larger. By the time you reach the centre of the loop the arcs of these large circles are almost straight lines. Apply the right-hand thumb rule to any small section of the loop: every section sends its field the same way through the inside of the loop. So at the centre the field lines are nearly parallel straight lines running perpendicular to the plane of the loop, all in one direction.

Activity 12.6 shows this pattern. Insert a circular coil of many turns through two holes in a cardboard so that the coil is perpendicular to the cardboard, connect it in series with a battery, a key and a rheostat, sprinkle iron filings, plug the key and tap the board. Around each wire the filings form circles; across the middle of the coil they line up as nearly straight parallel lines.

Two facts you must state: (i) the field at the centre of the loop is directly proportional to the current, and (ii) if the coil has n turns, the field is n times that of a single turn, because the current in every turn goes round in the same direction and the fields of the turns simply add. The field at the centre also increases if the radius of the loop is made smaller, because the centre is then closer to the wire.

Direction of the field, an NCERT in-text question: a loop lies flat on a table and the current goes round it clockwise as seen from above. Curl the right-hand fingers with the current; the thumb points downward. So inside the loop the field points downward, into the table, and outside the loop the field lines return upward, out of the table. For an anticlockwise current the field inside is upward. A useful memory aid: a clockwise current seen face-on makes that face a south pole, an anticlockwise current makes it a north pole.

formulas.expr: B<sub>centre</sub> ∝ n I (circular coil of n turns)
where: number of turns in the coil

sections.tip: NCERT exercise 3(a) says 'the field at the centre of a long circular coil will be parallel straight lines': this is TRUE. Students who remember 'circles' for a straight wire mark it false and lose the mark.

sections.heading: 12.2.4 Magnetic Field due to a Current in a Solenoid; the electromagnet
sections.body:
A solenoid is a coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wound closely in the shape of a cylinder. When current flows through it, the field pattern looks exactly like that of a bar magnet: lines emerge from one end, loop around outside and enter the other end. One end of the solenoid behaves as a north pole and the other as a south pole. You can find which is which with the right-hand thumb rule on one turn, or with the clockwise/anticlockwise trick: looking at an end, if the current goes anticlockwise, that end is a north pole; if clockwise, a south pole.

Inside the solenoid the field lines are parallel straight lines, equally spaced. This tells you the field inside a long solenoid is the same at every point, that is, it is uniform. This one sentence is the basis of the most repeated MCQ in the chapter: the field inside a long straight current-carrying solenoid is the same at all points, not zero, not more at the ends.

The strength of the field of a solenoid increases with (i) the current, (ii) the number of turns per unit length, and (iii) the presence of a soft iron core inside it. Put a rod of soft iron inside the solenoid while current flows and the strong uniform field magnetises it. The magnet so formed is an electromagnet. It is a temporary magnet: switch off the current and soft iron loses almost all its magnetism, which is exactly why soft iron and not steel is used for the core. Uses: electric bells, cranes for lifting scrap iron, loudspeakers, relays and MRI machines in hospitals.

The 2019 board question asks for two distinguishing features between the field of a solenoid and that of a bar magnet, so learn them: (1) the field inside a solenoid is uniform, while the field of a bar magnet is not uniform anywhere; (2) the field of a solenoid can be switched on and off, and its strength and polarity can be changed by changing the current, whereas a bar magnet's field is fixed. A third: the solenoid field lines pass through the hollow interior, whereas in a bar magnet they pass through the solid material from S to N.

formulas.expr: B<sub>inside</sub> ∝ n I (n = turns per unit length); same at all points inside
where: number of turns per unit length of the solenoid

sections.tip: Draw the solenoid as a helix with at least five turns, show current direction on the wire, mark N and S on the ends, draw lines inside as straight parallel arrows and outside as loops from N to S. Missing the arrows inside is the commonest lost mark.

sections.heading: 12.3 Force on a Current-carrying Conductor in a Magnetic Field (Activity 12.7, Fleming's left-hand rule)
sections.body:
A current produces a field that exerts a force on a nearby magnet. Ampere argued that the magnet must exert an equal and opposite force on the current-carrying conductor. Activity 12.7 demonstrates it and is the standard 3-mark or 5-mark 'describe an activity' item. Hang a small aluminium rod AB (about 5 cm) horizontally from a stand using two connecting wires. Place a strong horseshoe magnet so that the rod lies between its poles with the field directed upward: north pole vertically below the rod, south pole vertically above it. Connect the rod in series with a battery, a key and a rheostat and pass current from B to A. The rod is pushed sideways, to the left. Reverse the current and it moves to the right. Interchange the poles of the magnet (field downward) and the direction of displacement reverses again.

Conclusions: a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force; the direction of the force reverses if either the current or the field is reversed; the force is perpendicular to both the current and the field. Experiments also show the displacement is largest, that is, the force is maximum, when the current is at right angles to the field. When the current is parallel to the field, the force is zero.

Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand so that they are mutually perpendicular. If the forefinger points along the magnetic field and the middle finger along the current, the thumb gives the direction of the force (motion) on the conductor. Memory aid: F-B-I from thumb to middle finger: Force, B (field), I (current). Devices based on this force: electric motor, loudspeaker, microphone, galvanometer and other measuring instruments.

The examiner also tests moving charges, because a moving charge is a current. Direction of current is the direction of motion of a positive charge and opposite to the motion of an electron. Example 12.2: an electron enters a field at right angles; take the current opposite to the electron's velocity, then apply the rule. For a particle moving freely in a field the force is always perpendicular to its velocity, so it does no work: the particle's speed and kinetic energy stay the same, but the direction of its velocity, and hence its velocity and momentum, keep changing. A charge at rest, or moving parallel to the field, feels no force.

formulas.expr: F ∝ B I L sin θ; F is maximum when θ = 90°, zero when θ = 0°
where: length of conductor inside the field

sections.tip: Before applying Fleming's rule to an electron beam, convert to conventional current: current is opposite to the electron's motion. Applying the rule directly to the electron's velocity gives the opposite answer and zero marks.

sections.heading: 12.4 Domestic Electric Circuits
sections.body:
Electric power reaches a house through the mains, by overhead lines or underground cables. It comes as two wires: the live wire (red insulation) and the neutral wire (black insulation). In India the potential difference between them is 220 V, supplied as alternating current at 50 Hz. At the meter board the two wires pass through a main fuse into the electricity meter and then through the main switch to the line wires of the house.

Inside the house there are usually two separate circuits: a 15 A circuit for high-power appliances such as geysers, air coolers and heaters, and a 5 A circuit for bulbs, fans and similar loads. In each circuit every appliance is connected between the live and neutral wires, in parallel with the others, so that each gets the full 220 V and each has its own switch. The switch and the fuse are always placed in the live wire, so that when the switch is off or the fuse blows, the appliance is disconnected from the live line and is safe to touch.

The third wire is the earth wire (green insulation), connected to a metal plate buried deep in the earth near the house. The metallic body of appliances like an electric iron, toaster, table fan or refrigerator is connected to it. If insulation fails and current leaks to the body, the earth wire gives it a low-resistance path to the ground, keeping the body at earth potential; the leakage current flows to earth instead of through the person, and the large current usually blows the fuse as well.

An electric fuse is a short piece of wire of a metal or alloy with a suitable low melting point, connected in series in the live wire. If the current exceeds its rating, Joule heating melts the fuse and breaks the circuit. Two situations cause an unduly large current. Short-circuiting: the live and neutral wires come into direct contact (damaged insulation or a faulty appliance); the resistance of the path becomes very small and the current rises abruptly to a huge value. Overloading: the current exceeds the safe limit because too many appliances are connected to a single socket, or because of an accidental hike in supply voltage, or because a short circuit has occurred. Precautions: never connect too many high-power appliances to one socket, use a fuse (or MCB) of the correct rating, keep insulation in good condition, and use separate circuits for high-power appliances.

formulas.expr: I = P/V; choose a fuse rating just above I

sections.tip: A fuse must be replaced by one of the same rating. A higher-rated fuse will not melt in time and the appliance burns; a lower-rated one blows in normal use. This 'why the same rating' reasoning was a 2020 board question.

sections.heading: Background (not currently examinable): direct current, alternating current and its frequency
sections.body:
Direct current, alternating current, frequency of AC and the advantage of AC over DC were part of the old Electric Generator section of this chapter. The 2023 CBSE rationalisation removed the electric generator topic altogether, along with the electric motor and electromagnetic induction, and this DC/AC discussion went with it. It is not on the current syllabus and should not be expected as a stand-alone question in present-day board papers, even though it was asked often as a 1-mark or 2-mark item in papers before the rationalisation (hence the older years attached to this section). The rationalised NCERT text keeps only one line on the idea, in the closing summary of the chapter: our homes receive AC power of 220 V at a frequency of 50 Hz. That one line is still worth knowing, because Section 12.4 (Domestic Electric Circuits), which is on the syllabus, depends on it.

For background only: direct current (DC) flows in one direction only; its magnitude may vary but its direction does not. Sources: a dry cell, a car battery, a solar cell, a DC generator. Alternating current (AC) reverses its direction periodically; the mains supply in our homes is AC, produced by an AC generator at the power station.

The frequency of AC is the number of complete cycles per second. In India it is 50 Hz, which means 50 cycles in one second, so one cycle takes 1/50 s = 0.02 s. The current reverses direction twice in every cycle, once after each half-cycle, so it changes direction 100 times in one second, that is, once every 1/100 s = 0.01 s. Read the question carefully: 'how many cycles' is 50, 'how many times does it change direction' is 100.

The advantage once quoted for AC over DC was that it can be transmitted over long distances from the generating station to the consumer without much loss of electrical energy, because its voltage can be stepped up for transmission and stepped down for use. Keep this only as background; do not spend revision time on the deleted electric-generator material itself.

formulas.expr: T = 1/f; for f = 50 Hz, T = 0.02 s; direction reversals per second = 2f = 100

sections.tip: This topic is off the current syllabus. Only carry forward the one surviving fact for Section 12.4: the domestic supply is AC, 220 V, 50 Hz, reversing direction 100 times a second. If a question does ask for the frequency or reversal count, writing 'changes direction 50 times a second' is the standard mistake.

key_terms.definition: The region around a magnet (or a current-carrying conductor) in which its magnetic force can be detected. It has both magnitude and direction.

Curves used to represent a magnetic field; the path along which a free north pole would move. The tangent at a point gives the direction of the field there, and the closeness of lines shows the relative strength.
A small bar magnet pivoted at its centre so that it can turn freely; its north-seeking end points towards geographic north and it is used to find the direction of a magnetic field.
A field whose magnitude and direction are the same at every point of a region, represented by equally spaced parallel straight field lines, all pointing the same way.
Hold the current-carrying straight conductor in the right hand with the thumb along the current; the curled fingers give the direction of the magnetic field lines around it.
Another form of the right-hand thumb rule: if a right-handed corkscrew is driven forward along the current, the direction of rotation of its handle gives the direction of the magnetic field.
A coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wrapped closely in the shape of a cylinder. When it carries current its field resembles that of a bar magnet and is uniform inside.
A temporary magnet made by placing a soft iron core inside a current-carrying solenoid; its magnetism lasts only while the current flows.

With the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular, if the forefinger points along the magnetic field and the middle finger along the current, the thumb points along the force on the conductor.
The wire of the mains supply at high potential (220 V relative to neutral), usually with red insulation; switches and fuses are placed in it.
The return wire of the mains supply at approximately earth potential, usually with black insulation.

The wire with green insulation connected to a metal plate buried deep in the earth; it is joined to the metallic body of an appliance so that any leakage current flows to the earth instead of through the user.
A safety device: a short wire of a metal or alloy of low melting point, connected in series in the live wire, which melts and breaks the circuit when the current exceeds a safe value.
The situation when the live and neutral wires come into direct contact, so the resistance of the circuit falls sharply and the current rises abruptly to a very large value.
The condition in which the current in a circuit exceeds its safe rating, caused by connecting too many appliances to one socket, a rise in supply voltage, or a short circuit.
A current that reverses its direction periodically; the domestic supply in India is AC of 220 V at 50 Hz.
A current that flows in one direction only, such as the current from a cell or a battery.
The number of complete cycles the alternating current makes in one second, measured in hertz; 50 Hz in India.

formula_sheet.name: Field of a straight conductor
formula_sheet.note: Field at a point is directly proportional to the current and inversely proportional to the perpendicular distance from the wire; field lines are concentric circles.

formula_sheet.name: Direction around a straight wire
formula_sheet.expr: Right-hand thumb rule: thumb = current, curled fingers = field
formula_sheet.note: Current east to west: field is south below the wire and north above it. Current downward in a vertical wire: field clockwise seen from above.

formula_sheet.name: Field at the centre of a circular coil
formula_sheet.note: n turns add up because current in every turn circulates the same way; smaller radius gives a stronger field at the centre.

formula_sheet.name: Field inside a solenoid
formula_sheet.expr: B ∝ n I (n = turns per unit length), uniform inside
formula_sheet.note: Increased by more current, more turns per unit length, and a soft iron core.

formula_sheet.name: Force on a current-carrying conductor
formula_sheet.expr: F ∝ B I L sin θ
formula_sheet.note: Maximum when the conductor is perpendicular to the field (θ = 90°), zero when parallel (θ = 0°). Direction from Fleming's left-hand rule.

formula_sheet.name: Fleming's left-hand rule
formula_sheet.expr: Forefinger = B, middle finger = I, thumb = F (left hand)
formula_sheet.note: For an electron beam, take the current opposite to the electron's motion before applying the rule.

formula_sheet.name: Current drawn by an appliance
formula_sheet.note: V = 220 V in India. 2 kW oven: I = 2000/220 = 9.09 A, so it cannot run on a 5 A circuit.

formula_sheet.name: Fuse rating
formula_sheet.expr: Fuse rating slightly greater than I = P/V
formula_sheet.note: Always in series in the live wire; replace with the same rating.

formula_sheet.name: Time period of AC
formula_sheet.note: Direction reverses twice per cycle, so 2f = 100 reversals per second at 50 Hz.

formula_sheet.name: Domestic circuit ratings
formula_sheet.expr: 220 V, 50 Hz; 15 A line for heavy appliances, 5 A line for bulbs and fans
formula_sheet.note: Appliances are in parallel across live and neutral so each gets 220 V and has its own switch.

diagrams.title: Magnetic field lines around a bar magnet
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a rectangle for the magnet with N on the left end and S on the right. Draw five or six smooth curves starting at N, bulging outward and ending at S, with arrowheads pointing from N to S outside the magnet. Draw the lines closer together near the poles. Inside the magnet draw a few short arrows from S to N to show that the lines are closed curves.

diagrams.title: Field lines of a straight current-carrying conductor (Activity 12.5)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a vertical wire passing through a horizontal cardboard sheet, with a battery, key and rheostat connected below. On the cardboard draw three or four concentric circles centred on the wire, spaced wider as they go out. Mark the direction of current on the wire with an arrow and put an arrowhead on each circle following the right-hand thumb rule (anticlockwise seen from above for upward current). Show a compass on one circle with its north pole along the arrow.

diagrams.title: Field lines through and around a current-carrying solenoid
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a helix of five to seven turns with the current direction marked on the wire and the battery at one side. Label the two ends N and S. Inside the solenoid draw straight, parallel, equally spaced lines with arrows from S towards N. Outside draw curved lines leaving N, looping around and entering S. Write 'uniform field inside' beside the parallel lines.

diagrams.title: Fleming's left-hand rule
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a left hand with the thumb pointing up, the forefinger pointing forward and the middle finger pointing to the right, the three mutually perpendicular. Label forefinger 'magnetic field (B)', middle finger 'current (I)' and thumb 'force / motion (F)'. Write 'left hand' clearly; an unlabelled hand earns nothing.

diagrams.title: Activity 12.7: force on a current-carrying aluminium rod
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a horizontal rod AB hanging from a stand by two wires, connected to a battery, key and rheostat. Draw a horseshoe magnet with its N pole below the rod and S pole above it, and an arrow labelled 'B, upward' between the poles. Mark the current from B to A on the rod and an arrow showing the rod displaced sideways, labelled 'force'.

diagrams.title: Schematic of a domestic electric circuit
diagrams.how_to_draw: From the left draw three incoming wires: live (red, L), neutral (black, N) and earth (green, E). Pass L and N through the main fuse, then the electricity meter, then the main switch, to a distribution board. From the board draw two circuits: a 15 A line with a fuse feeding a geyser socket, and a 5 A line with a fuse feeding a bulb and a fan, each appliance connected between L and N in parallel with its own switch on the live side. Connect the earth wire to the metal body of one appliance and to an 'earth plate' drawn below ground.

ncert_questions.q: Why does a compass needle get deflected when brought near a bar magnet?
ncert_questions.a: A compass needle is itself a small bar magnet with a north and a south pole. A bar magnet has a magnetic field in the region around it. When the compass is brought into this field, its poles experience forces (the north pole of the needle is attracted by the south pole of the magnet and repelled by its north pole), and the needle turns until it lies along the field line at that point. That turning is the deflection.

ncert_questions.q: List the properties of magnetic field lines.
ncert_questions.a:
(i) Outside a magnet the field lines emerge from the north pole and merge into the south pole; inside the magnet they go from south to north, so the lines form closed curves.
(ii) The direction of the field at a point is given by the tangent to the field line at that point, the direction in which a free north pole would move.
(iii) The field is stronger where the lines are crowded together (near the poles) and weaker where they are far apart.
(iv) No two field lines cross each other, because at the crossing point the field would have two directions, which is impossible.

ncert_questions.q: Why don't two magnetic field lines intersect each other?
ncert_questions.a: The direction of the magnetic field at a point is the direction of the tangent to the field line through that point. If two field lines intersected, there would be two tangents and hence two directions of the field at the same point. A compass needle placed there would have to point in two directions at once, which is not possible. So field lines never intersect.

ncert_questions.q: Consider a circular loop of wire lying in the plane of the table. Let the current pass through the loop clockwise. Apply the right-hand rule to find out the direction of the magnetic field inside and outside the loop.
ncert_questions.a: Apply the right-hand thumb rule to a small section of the loop: with the thumb along the current, the fingers curl around that section. For a clockwise current (seen from above) every section sends its field downward through the inside of the loop and upward outside it. So inside the loop the field points vertically downward, into the table, and outside the loop the field lines come out of the table and point upward. The top face of the loop behaves as a south pole.

ncert_questions.q: The magnetic field in a given region is uniform. Draw a diagram to represent it.
ncert_questions.a: A uniform field has the same magnitude and direction at every point. It is represented by straight, parallel field lines that are equally spaced, all carrying arrowheads in the same direction. For example, five horizontal lines of equal length, one below the other with equal gaps, each with an arrow pointing to the right.

ncert_questions.q: Choose the correct option. The magnetic field inside a long straight solenoid-carrying current (a) is zero (b) decreases as we move towards its end (c) increases as we move towards its end (d) is the same at all points.
ncert_questions.a: (d) is the same at all points. Inside a long current-carrying solenoid the field lines are parallel straight lines, equally spaced, which means the field is uniform: same magnitude and same direction at every point inside.

ncert_questions.q: Which of the following property of a proton can change while it moves freely in a magnetic field? (There may be more than one correct answer.) (a) mass (b) speed (c) velocity (d) momentum
ncert_questions.a: (c) velocity and (d) momentum. The force on a moving charge in a magnetic field is always perpendicular to its velocity, so it does no work and cannot change the speed or kinetic energy; the mass is a constant anyway. But the force keeps changing the direction of motion, so the velocity (a vector) changes, and hence the momentum (mass × velocity) also changes.

ncert_questions.q: In Activity 12.7, how do we think the displacement of rod AB will be affected if (i) current in rod AB is increased; (ii) a stronger horse-shoe magnet is used; and (iii) length of the rod AB is increased?
ncert_questions.a: The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field increases with the current, the strength of the field and the length of the conductor in the field. So in all three cases the force increases and the displacement of the rod becomes larger: (i) larger current, larger displacement; (ii) stronger magnet, larger displacement; (iii) longer rod inside the field, larger displacement. The direction of the displacement does not change in any of the three cases.

ncert_questions.q: A positively-charged particle (alpha-particle) projected towards west is deflected towards north by a magnetic field. The direction of magnetic field is (a) towards south (b) towards east (c) downward (d) upward
ncert_questions.a: (d) upward. The alpha particle is positive, so the current is in its direction of motion, towards the west. The force is towards the north. Apply Fleming's left-hand rule: point the middle finger west (current) and the thumb north (force); the forefinger then points vertically upward, which is the direction of the field.

ncert_questions.q: Name two safety measures commonly used in electric circuits and appliances.
ncert_questions.a:
(i) An electric fuse (or a miniature circuit breaker, MCB) of the proper rating connected in series in the live wire, which breaks the circuit when the current exceeds the safe limit due to overloading or short-circuiting.
(ii) Earthing: the metallic body of an appliance is connected to the earth wire so that any leakage current passes to the earth and the user does not get a shock.

ncert_questions.q: An electric oven of 2 kW power rating is operated in a domestic electric circuit (220 V) that has a current rating of 5 A. What result do you expect? Explain.
ncert_questions.a:
Current drawn by the oven: I = P/V = 2000 W / 220 V = 9.09 A (about 9.1 A).
This is much more than the 5 A rating of the circuit. The current through the fuse exceeds its rating, so the fuse wire heats up, melts and breaks the circuit. The oven will not work, and if there were no fuse the wiring would overheat and could catch fire. The oven should be connected to the 15 A circuit meant for high-power appliances.

ncert_questions.q: What precaution should be taken to avoid the overloading of domestic electric circuits?
ncert_questions.a:
(i) Do not connect too many appliances, especially high-power ones, to a single socket at the same time.
(ii) Use a fuse or MCB of the correct rating in each circuit so that it breaks the circuit when the current exceeds the safe value.
(iii) Connect high-power appliances such as geysers and heaters only to the separate 15 A circuit, and keep the 5 A circuit for lights and fans.
(iv) Keep wiring and insulation in good condition so that short circuits do not occur.

ncert_questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the magnetic field near a long straight wire? (a) The field consists of straight lines perpendicular to the wire. (b) The field consists of straight lines parallel to the wire. (c) The field consists of radial lines originating from the wire. (d) The field consists of concentric circles centred on the wire.
ncert_questions.a: (d) The field consists of concentric circles centred on the wire. Iron filings sprinkled around a vertical current-carrying wire arrange themselves in concentric circles, and a compass placed on any circle points along the tangent to it.

ncert_questions.q: At the time of short circuit, the current in the circuit (a) reduces substantially (b) does not change (c) increases heavily (d) vary continuously.
ncert_questions.a: (c) increases heavily. In a short circuit the live and neutral wires touch directly, the resistance of the path becomes very small, and by Ohm's law the current rises abruptly to a very large value.

ncert_questions.q: State whether the following statements are true or false. (a) The field at the centre of a long circular coil carrying current will be parallel straight lines. (b) A wire with a green insulation is usually the live wire of an electric supply.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) True. At the centre of a circular coil the arcs of the large concentric circles around each part of the wire appear as nearly straight parallel lines, all in the same direction.
(b) False. The wire with green insulation is the earth wire. The live wire usually has red insulation and the neutral wire black.

ncert_questions.q: List two methods of producing magnetic fields.
ncert_questions.a:
(i) By a permanent magnet, such as a bar magnet or a horseshoe magnet; the region around it has a magnetic field.
(ii) By passing an electric current through a conductor: a straight wire, a circular coil or a solenoid all produce a magnetic field while current flows (an electromagnet is the strongest example).

ncert_questions.q: When is the force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field largest?
ncert_questions.a: The force is largest when the direction of the current in the conductor is at right angles (perpendicular) to the direction of the magnetic field. The force is zero when the current is parallel to the field.

ncert_questions.q: Imagine that you are sitting in a chamber with your back to one wall. An electron beam, moving horizontally from back wall towards the front wall, is deflected by a strong magnetic field to your right side. What is the direction of magnetic field?
ncert_questions.a: The electrons move from the back wall towards the front wall, so the conventional current is in the opposite direction: from the front wall towards the back wall. The force on the beam is towards the right. Apply Fleming's left-hand rule: middle finger pointing backward (current), thumb pointing to the right (force). The forefinger then points vertically downward. So the magnetic field is directed vertically downward.

ncert_questions.q: State the rule to determine the direction of a (i) magnetic field produced around a straight conductor-carrying current, (ii) force experienced by a current-carrying straight conductor placed in a magnetic field which is perpendicular to it, and (iii) current induced in a coil due to its rotation in a magnetic field.
ncert_questions.a:
(i) Right-hand thumb rule: hold the conductor in the right hand with the thumb along the current; the curled fingers give the direction of the field lines around the conductor.
(ii) Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular; if the forefinger points along the field and the middle finger along the current, the thumb points along the force on the conductor.
(iii) Fleming's right-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the right hand mutually perpendicular; if the forefinger points along the field and the thumb along the motion of the conductor, the middle finger gives the direction of the induced current. (Part (iii) belongs to electromagnetic induction, which has been removed from the syllabus, so learn only the statement.)

ncert_questions.q: When does an electric short circuit occur?
ncert_questions.a: A short circuit occurs when the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact with each other, either because the insulation of the wires is damaged or because there is a fault in an appliance. The resistance of the circuit then becomes very small, so the current abruptly increases to a very large value. The resulting heating can damage the wiring and cause a fire; a fuse in the live wire melts and breaks the circuit to prevent this.

ncert_questions.q: What is the function of an earth wire? Why is it necessary to earth metallic appliances?
ncert_questions.a:
Function: the earth wire (green insulation) connects the metallic body of an appliance to a metal plate buried deep in the earth. It provides a low-resistance conducting path from the body of the appliance to the earth.
Why necessary: if the insulation inside an appliance fails and the live wire touches the metal body, the body would otherwise be at 220 V and anyone touching it would receive a severe shock. With earthing, the leakage current flows through the earth wire to the ground, keeping the body at the potential of the earth, and the large current usually blows the fuse as well. So earthing protects the user from electric shock.

pyq.q: The strength of magnetic field inside a long current-carrying straight solenoid is
options: more at the ends than at the centre
found to increase from one end to the other
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The field lines inside a long solenoid are parallel, equally spaced straight lines, so the field is uniform: same magnitude and direction at all points inside.

pyq.q: At the time of a short circuit, the current in the circuit
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The live and neutral wires touch directly, the resistance of the path drops to nearly zero, so the current rises to a very large value.

pyq.q: A current-carrying conductor is held vertically. To produce a magnetic field that is clockwise when viewed from above, the current in the conductor should flow
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: By the right-hand thumb rule, when the thumb (current) points downward, the fingers curl clockwise as seen from above. For an upward current the field would be anticlockwise from above.

pyq.q: A horizontal power line carries current from east to west. The direction of the magnetic field at a point directly below the line is
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Apply the right-hand thumb rule with the thumb pointing west: the field circles the wire so that it points south directly below the wire and north directly above it (NCERT Example 12.1).

pyq.q: Which of the following statements about magnetic field lines is NOT correct?
options: They emerge from the north pole and merge at the south pole outside the magnet
They are crowded near the poles where the field is strong
Two field lines can intersect where the field is very strong
Inside the magnet they run from the south pole to the north pole
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Field lines never intersect, whatever the strength of the field; at a crossing point a compass would have to point in two directions at once.

pyq.q: A proton moves freely in a uniform magnetic field. Which of its properties remains unchanged?
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: The magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work; the speed and kinetic energy stay constant while the direction, and hence velocity and momentum, change.

pyq.q: In a domestic electric circuit, the fuse and the switch of an appliance are connected in the
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Both are placed in the live wire so that when the switch is off or the fuse blows, the appliance is cut off from the high-potential line and is safe to touch.

pyq.q: The frequency of the alternating current supplied to houses in India is 50 Hz. The number of times the current changes its direction in one second is
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The current reverses direction twice in every cycle, so with 50 cycles per second it reverses 2 × 50 = 100 times per second.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Two magnetic field lines never intersect each other. Reason (R): At the point of intersection the magnetic field would have two directions, which is not possible.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The tangent to a field line gives the field direction; two tangents at one point would mean two directions, so lines cannot cross. R explains A directly.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The magnetic field inside a long current-carrying solenoid is uniform. Reason (R): The field lines inside the solenoid are parallel straight lines, equally spaced.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Parallel, equally spaced lines mean the same direction and the same magnitude at every point, which is what uniform means, so R is the correct explanation of A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): A charged particle moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences no force. Reason (R): The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is largest when the current is perpendicular to the field.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Both statements are true, but R describes the maximum-force condition; it does not explain why the force is zero for parallel motion (that follows from F ∝ sin θ being zero at θ = 0°).

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The earth wire is connected to the metallic body of an electric iron. Reason (R): The earth wire carries the normal working current of the appliance back to the power station.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The body is earthed for safety, so A is true. The earth wire carries only leakage current to the ground; the working current returns through the neutral wire, so R is false.

pyq.q: A compass needle is placed near a current-carrying straight conductor. State what happens to the deflection of the needle if (i) the current in the conductor is increased, and (ii) the compass is moved away from the conductor while the current is kept the same. Give reasons.
pyq.answer:
(i) The deflection increases, because the magnetic field at a point near the conductor is directly proportional to the current; a larger current produces a stronger field, which exerts a larger turning force on the needle. (1 mark)
(ii) The deflection decreases, because the field of a straight conductor is inversely proportional to the distance from it; farther from the wire the field is weaker. (1 mark)

pyq.q: What is an electromagnet? List any two uses.
pyq.answer:
An electromagnet is a temporary magnet formed when a piece of soft iron is placed inside a current-carrying solenoid; the strong field inside the solenoid magnetises the soft iron, and the magnetism disappears when the current is switched off. (1 mark)
Uses (any two): electric bells; cranes for lifting heavy pieces of scrap iron; loudspeakers and microphones; relays and electric motors; MRI machines. (1 mark)

pyq.q: What is the frequency of the AC supply in India? How many times does this current change its direction in one second?
pyq.answer:
The frequency of the domestic AC supply in India is 50 Hz, that is, 50 complete cycles per second, each cycle lasting 1/50 s = 0.02 s. (1 mark)
The current changes its direction twice in every cycle (once after each half cycle), so it changes direction 2 × 50 = 100 times in one second, once every 0.01 s. (1 mark)

pyq.q: A fuse wire in a circuit has blown. Why should it be replaced with a fuse wire of the same rating and not of a higher rating?
pyq.answer: The rating of a fuse is the maximum current it allows before it melts, chosen just above the normal current of the circuit. (½ mark) If a fuse of a higher rating is used, it will not melt when the current exceeds the safe limit of the circuit; the wiring and appliances will carry a dangerously large current, overheat and may catch fire. (1 mark) So the blown fuse must be replaced by one of the same rating so that the circuit is again protected at the correct current. (½ mark)

pyq.q: State the right-hand thumb rule. A current flows from south to north in a horizontal wire. What is the direction of the magnetic field at a point directly above the wire?
pyq.answer:
Right-hand thumb rule: hold the current-carrying straight conductor in the right hand so that the thumb points along the current; the curled fingers then point along the direction of the magnetic field lines around the conductor. (1 mark)
With the thumb pointing north, the fingers above the wire curl from west to east: at a point directly above the wire the field points towards the east (and towards the west directly below it). (1 mark)

pyq.q: What is a solenoid? Draw the pattern of magnetic field lines of (i) a current-carrying solenoid and (ii) a bar magnet. List two distinguishing features between the two fields.
pyq.answer:
A solenoid is a coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wound closely in the shape of a cylinder. (½ mark)
Diagrams: (i) a helix with current marked, N and S at the ends, parallel straight arrows inside and closed loops outside from N to S; (ii) a bar magnet with lines leaving N, curving round and entering S, crowded near the poles. (1 mark)
Distinguishing features (any two): (1) inside a solenoid the field is uniform (parallel, equally spaced lines), whereas the field of a bar magnet is non-uniform, strongest near the poles; (2) the solenoid's field exists only while current flows and its strength and polarity can be changed by changing the current, whereas a bar magnet's field is permanent and fixed; (3) the solenoid's field lines pass through its hollow interior, whereas in a bar magnet they pass through the solid material from S to N. (1½ marks)

pyq.q: Name the factors on which the force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field depends. When is this force maximum? State the rule that gives its direction, and explain what happens to the direction of the force if (i) the current is reversed, and (ii) the magnetic field is reversed.
pyq.answer:
Factors: the strength of the magnetic field, the current in the conductor, the length of the conductor inside the field, and the angle between the current and the field. (1 mark)
The force is maximum when the current is perpendicular to the magnetic field, and zero when it is parallel. (½ mark)
Direction: Fleming's left-hand rule; with the forefinger along the field and the middle finger along the current, the thumb of the left hand gives the force. (1 mark)
(i) Reversing the current reverses the direction of the force; (ii) reversing the field also reverses the direction of the force. (½ mark)

pyq.q: An alpha particle is (i) at rest, (ii) moving parallel to a magnetic field, (iii) moving perpendicular to a magnetic field. In which case(s) does it experience a force? Give reasons.
pyq.answer:
An alpha particle is a positively charged particle, and a moving charge is equivalent to a current in the direction of its motion. (½ mark)
(i) At rest: no force, because a stationary charge is not a current and a magnetic field acts only on moving charges. (½ mark)
(ii) Moving parallel to the field: no force, because the force on a current-carrying conductor is zero when the current is parallel to the field (angle 0°). (1 mark)
(iii) Moving perpendicular to the field: it experiences the maximum force, perpendicular to both its velocity and the field, in the direction given by Fleming's left-hand rule; this force changes the direction of motion but not the speed. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Describe an activity to show that the magnetic field lines around a straight current-carrying conductor are concentric circles. How does the field vary with distance from the conductor?
pyq.answer:
Activity: pass a long thick copper wire vertically through the centre of a horizontal cardboard; connect it in series with a battery, a rheostat, an ammeter and a plug key. Sprinkle iron filings uniformly on the cardboard, close the key and tap the cardboard gently. (1 mark)
Observation: the filings arrange in concentric circles centred on the wire; these are the field lines. A compass placed on any circle points along the circle, and its direction reverses when the current is reversed. (1 mark)
Variation with distance: the circles become larger and farther apart as we move away from the wire, and the compass deflection at a farther point is smaller; the field is inversely proportional to the distance from the conductor. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Why is the live wire more dangerous than the neutral wire? Why are domestic appliances connected in parallel? What is the importance of a fuse in a domestic circuit?
pyq.answer:
The live wire is at a high potential of 220 V with respect to the earth, whereas the neutral wire is at nearly the potential of the earth; touching the live wire drives a large current through the body, so it is more dangerous. (1 mark)
Appliances are connected in parallel so that each gets the full 220 V supply, each can be switched on or off independently, and a fault in one does not stop the others. (1 mark)
A fuse, connected in series in the live wire, melts and breaks the circuit when the current exceeds its rating due to overloading or a short circuit, protecting the wiring and appliances from damage and fire. (1 mark)

pyq.q: (a) State Fleming's left-hand rule. (b) Describe an activity to show that a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force. (c) State the characteristics of the AC supply received at homes in India. (d) What is a fuse? Why is earthing of metallic appliances necessary?
pyq.answer:
(a) Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand so that they are mutually perpendicular. If the forefinger points along the magnetic field and the middle finger along the current, then the thumb points in the direction of the force (motion) on the conductor. (1 mark)

(b) Suspend a small aluminium rod AB horizontally from a stand with two connecting wires. Place a strong horseshoe magnet so that the rod lies between its poles, north pole below and south pole above, giving an upward field. Connect the rod in series with a battery, key and rheostat and pass current from B to A. The rod is displaced to one side (to the left). Reversing the current displaces it to the right; interchanging the poles also reverses the displacement. This shows that a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force whose direction depends on the directions of both the current and the field. (2 marks)

(c) The supply is alternating current with a potential difference of 220 V between live and neutral, at a frequency of 50 Hz; the current reverses direction 100 times every second. (1 mark)

(d) A fuse is a short wire of a metal or alloy of low melting point connected in series in the live wire; it melts and breaks the circuit when the current exceeds its rating. Earthing is necessary because if the live wire touches the metal body of an appliance, the earth wire provides a low-resistance path for the leakage current to the ground, keeping the body at earth potential so the user does not get a severe shock. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Draw a schematic labelled diagram of a domestic wiring circuit which includes (i) a main fuse, (ii) a power meter, (iii) one light point and (iv) a power plug. Distinguish between short circuiting and overloading. What precautions should be taken to avoid overloading?
pyq.answer:
Diagram: draw the live (red), neutral (black) and earth (green) wires entering from the mains; take live and neutral through the main fuse, then the electricity meter, then the main switch to a distribution board. Show a 5 A circuit with its own fuse feeding a bulb with a switch in the live wire, and a 15 A circuit with its own fuse feeding a three-pin power socket whose third pin is joined to the earth wire; label every part. (2 marks)

Short circuiting: the live and neutral wires come into direct contact (damaged insulation or a faulty appliance); the resistance of the circuit falls almost to zero and the current abruptly rises to a very large value. Overloading: the current in a circuit exceeds its safe rating because too many appliances are connected to one socket, or the supply voltage rises accidentally, or a short circuit occurs; the wires overheat. A short circuit is one cause of overloading. (2 marks)

Precautions: do not connect many high-power appliances to a single socket; connect heavy appliances only to the 15 A circuit; use fuses or MCBs of the correct rating in every circuit; keep insulation and appliances in good repair. (1 mark)

pyq.q: (a) What is a solenoid? Draw the field lines of a current-carrying solenoid and state two properties of the field inside it. (b) How can a solenoid be used to make an electromagnet? Why is soft iron used as the core? (c) State three ways of increasing the strength of the magnetic field of a solenoid.
pyq.answer:
(a) A solenoid is a coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wound closely in the form of a cylinder. Diagram: helix with current direction, N and S marked at the ends, straight parallel arrows inside, closed loops outside from N to S. Properties of the field inside: it is uniform, the same at all points, and its direction is along the axis from the S end to the N end; the pattern resembles that of a bar magnet. (2 marks)

(b) Place a rod of soft iron inside the solenoid and pass current through the coil; the strong uniform field magnetises the rod, giving an electromagnet. Soft iron is used because it is magnetised strongly by the field and loses its magnetism as soon as the current stops, so the electromagnet can be switched on and off; steel would retain magnetism and become a permanent magnet. (2 marks)

(c) Increase the current through the solenoid; increase the number of turns per unit length; insert a soft iron core inside the solenoid. (1 mark)

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. In a physics laboratory, a student winds 200 turns of insulated copper wire closely on a hollow cardboard tube 20 cm long and connects it to a battery through a key and a rheostat. When the key is closed and a compass is moved around the tube, the needle behaves exactly as it does around a bar magnet. She then places an iron nail inside the tube; the nail picks up pins while the current flows and drops them when the key is opened. A second student says that pushing a bar of steel into the tube instead would give a better magnet.
(i) What is the arrangement of wire on the tube called? Name the type of magnet formed with the nail inside.
(ii) Why does the nail drop the pins when the key is opened?
(iii) Is the second student right? Give a reason.
(iv) The student doubles the current using the rheostat. What happens to the field inside the tube, and where inside the tube is the field strongest?
pyq.answer:
(i) The coil is a solenoid. With the iron nail inside it becomes an electromagnet. (1 mark)

(ii) The nail is made of soft iron, which is magnetised only while the current flows in the solenoid; when the key is opened the field disappears and the soft iron loses its magnetism, so it no longer attracts the pins. (1 mark)

(iii) No. Steel retains its magnetism after the current stops and would become a permanent magnet, so it cannot be switched off; for an electromagnet soft iron is the right core. (1 mark)

(iv) The field inside the solenoid is directly proportional to the current, so doubling the current doubles the field. The field inside a long solenoid is uniform, the same at all points, so there is no single strongest point inside. (1 mark)

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A family's kitchen has a single 5 A socket on the lighting circuit of the house. During winter they plug a 1000 W room heater, a 750 W electric iron and an 800 W toaster into it through a multi-plug at the same time. After a few minutes the fuse blows. An electrician later finds that the metal body of the iron gives a mild shock and that its three-pin plug has a broken third pin. The supply is 220 V, 50 Hz.
(i) Calculate the total current drawn by the three appliances and explain why the fuse blew.
(ii) Name the fault that occurred. How is it different from a short circuit?
(iii) Why did the metal body of the iron give a shock, and which wire was missing?
(iv) Suggest two changes the electrician should make.
pyq.answer:
(i) Total power = 1000 + 750 + 800 = 2550 W. Current I = P/V = 2550/220 = 11.6 A. This is far above the 5 A rating of the circuit, so the fuse wire overheated, melted and broke the circuit. (1 mark)

(ii) The fault is overloading: too many appliances were connected to one socket so the current exceeded the safe rating. In a short circuit the live and neutral wires touch directly and the current rises abruptly to a very large value because the resistance becomes nearly zero; here the wires did not touch, the load was simply too large. (1 mark)

(iii) The broken third pin means the earth wire was not connected to the body of the iron. A small leakage of current from the live wire to the metal body had no path to the ground, so the body stayed at a high potential and current passed through the person touching it. (1 mark)

(iv) Replace the plug so that the earth pin connects the body to the earth wire; connect the heater and other high-power appliances to the separate 15 A circuit, not the 5 A lighting socket; do not use a multi-plug for several heavy appliances; fit a fuse or MCB of the correct rating. (any two, 1 mark)

options: a magnet produces an electric current
an electric current produces a magnetic field
a compass needle always points north
iron filings are attracted by copper
practice_mcq.explanation: In 1820 Oersted found a compass needle deflected when current flowed through a nearby wire, showing that a current produces a magnetic field.

practice_mcq.q: The direction of the magnetic field at a point is the direction in which
options: a south pole placed there would move
a north pole placed there would move
iron filings placed there would move
a positive charge at rest there would move
practice_mcq.explanation: By convention the field direction is the direction of the force on a north pole, which is the way the north pole of a compass needle points.

practice_mcq.q: Where the magnetic field lines are closer together,
practice_mcq.explanation: The degree of closeness of field lines shows the relative strength; lines crowd together near the poles where the field is strongest.

practice_mcq.q: Inside a bar magnet, the direction of the magnetic field lines is
options: from north pole to south pole
from south pole to north pole
perpendicular to the axis of the magnet
there are no field lines inside a magnet
practice_mcq.explanation: Outside the magnet the lines go from N to S; inside they return from S to N, which is what makes them closed curves.

practice_mcq.q: A straight wire carries current vertically upward. Viewed from above, the magnetic field lines around it are
options: straight lines parallel to the wire
practice_mcq.explanation: Right-hand thumb rule: thumb up, fingers curl anticlockwise as seen from above.

practice_mcq.q: If the current in a straight conductor is doubled and the distance of a point from it is also doubled, the magnetic field at that point
practice_mcq.explanation: B is directly proportional to I and inversely proportional to r; doubling both leaves B unchanged.

practice_mcq.q: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil carrying current increases when
options: the number of turns is decreased
the radius of the coil is increased
the number of turns is increased
practice_mcq.explanation: The fields of the individual turns add, so a coil of n turns gives n times the field of one turn; a smaller radius or larger current also increases it.

practice_mcq.q: Looking at one end of a current-carrying solenoid, the current appears anticlockwise. That end is
options: neither, a solenoid has no poles
a north pole only if a core is present
practice_mcq.explanation: An anticlockwise current seen face-on makes that face a north pole; a clockwise current makes it a south pole.

practice_mcq.q: The core of an electromagnet is made of soft iron rather than steel because soft iron
options: loses its magnetism as soon as the current stops
does not get magnetised at all
practice_mcq.explanation: An electromagnet must switch off with the current; soft iron is strongly magnetised while current flows and demagnetises when it stops, unlike steel.

practice_mcq.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, the middle finger represents the direction of
practice_mcq.explanation: Forefinger gives the field, middle finger the current and thumb the force or motion.

practice_mcq.q: An electron moving towards the east enters a magnetic field directed vertically upward. The force on the electron is directed
practice_mcq.explanation: The current is opposite to the electron's motion, so it is towards the west. Middle finger west, forefinger up: the thumb of the left hand points north.

practice_mcq.q: A current-carrying conductor experiences no force in a magnetic field when the current is
practice_mcq.explanation: The force is proportional to sin θ; it is zero for parallel (θ = 0°) and maximum for perpendicular (θ = 90°).

practice_mcq.q: In the domestic supply in India, the wire with black insulation is the
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT gives red for live, black for neutral and green for earth.

practice_mcq.q: The potential difference between the live and neutral wires of the domestic supply in India is
practice_mcq.explanation: The domestic supply is 220 V AC at 50 Hz.

practice_mcq.q: A 1500 W geyser is used on the 220 V supply. The most suitable fuse rating for its circuit is
practice_mcq.explanation: I = P/V = 1500/220 = 6.8 A. The fuse should be rated just above this, so 10 A; 5 A would blow in normal use and 15 A would not protect the geyser.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT a cause of overloading of a domestic circuit?
options: connecting many high-power appliances to one socket
an accidental rise in supply voltage
practice_mcq.explanation: Parallel connection is the normal, correct way to wire appliances; the other three all push the current beyond the safe rating.

practice_mcq.q: A circular coil of n turns carrying current I produces a magnetic field B at its centre. If the number of turns is doubled and the current is halved, the new field at the centre is
practice_mcq.explanation: The field at the centre of a coil is proportional to nI. Doubling n and halving I leaves the product nI, and hence the field, unchanged at B.

common_mistakes: Using the right-hand thumb rule to find the force on a conductor, or Fleming's left-hand rule to find the field of a wire. The two rules answer different questions; the examiner marks a rule as wrong even if the final direction happens to be right.

Applying Fleming's left-hand rule directly to the motion of an electron. The middle finger must point along conventional current, which is opposite to the electron's velocity; forgetting this flips the answer.

Writing that the field inside a solenoid is 'maximum at the centre' or 'zero'. NCERT says it is the same at all points inside; this is the single most repeated MCQ and Assertion–Reason in the chapter.
Drawing solenoid or straight-wire field lines without arrowheads, or without marking the direction of current on the wire. The direction mark is a separate marking point and is lost every time.

Answering 'why do field lines not intersect' with 'because they are closed curves'. The reason is that the field would have two directions at the crossing point, so a compass would point two ways at once.

Saying a short circuit and overloading are the same thing. A short circuit is live and neutral touching, with a near-zero resistance; overloading is any situation in which the current exceeds the rating, of which a short circuit is only one cause.
Placing the fuse or switch in the neutral wire in the circuit diagram. Both must be in the live wire so that the appliance is disconnected from the high-potential line when off.
Reporting that 50 Hz AC changes direction 50 times a second. It reverses twice per cycle, so 100 times a second.
Describing the earth wire as carrying the return current. It carries only leakage current from a faulty appliance to the ground; the neutral wire carries the return current.
strategy:
This is a short chapter after rationalisation, so prepare it completely; the questions are predictable and a full 4 to 6 marks is realistic. Spend one sitting on the three field patterns: bar magnet, straight wire and solenoid. Draw each one from memory three times with arrows, current direction and poles marked, because a diagram question comes almost every year. Then learn the four properties of field lines as four separate lines, with the 'two directions at one point' reason attached to the non-intersection property.

Spend the second sitting on rules and directions. Practise the right-hand thumb rule on the two stock cases (east-west horizontal wire, vertical wire seen from above) and Fleming's left-hand rule on the three stock cases (rod in a horseshoe magnet, electron beam, alpha particle). Always convert an electron's motion to conventional current first. Write down the two activities (12.5 with iron filings and 12.7 with the aluminium rod) as set-up, observation, conclusion, variation, in that order, since that is how the marking scheme allots points.

The third sitting is domestic circuits. Draw the schematic with live, neutral, earth, main fuse, meter, main switch and the 15 A and 5 A lines. Be able to write, in two lines each, the functions of the fuse and the earth wire, the definitions of short circuit and overloading, and three precautions. Practise I = P/V with the 2 kW oven on the 5 A line and pick a fuse rating from the answer. Finally, memorise the AC facts: 220 V, 50 Hz, 0.02 s per cycle, 100 reversals per second, and the long-distance transmission advantage. In the exam, give this chapter's 1-mark items thirty seconds each and a 3-mark diagram question about five minutes, including the drawing.
revision_checklist: I can describe Oersted's observation and state its two conclusions.
I can draw the field lines of a bar magnet and list four properties of field lines.
I can explain in one sentence why two field lines never intersect.
I can draw a uniform magnetic field.
I can describe Activity 12.5 (iron filings around a vertical wire) with set-up, observation and both variations.
I can state the right-hand thumb rule and give the field direction above and below an east-west wire.
I can explain why the field at the centre of a loop is nearly straight and how it depends on n and I.
I can draw the solenoid field, mark its poles, and state that the field inside is uniform.
I can define an electromagnet, say why soft iron is used, and list three ways to strengthen the field.
I can describe Activity 12.7 (aluminium rod in a horseshoe magnet) and its conclusions.
I can state Fleming's left-hand rule and apply it to an electron beam and to an alpha particle.
I know that speed stays constant but velocity and momentum change for a charge moving in a field.
I can draw the domestic circuit schematic with live, neutral, earth, main fuse, meter, 15 A and 5 A lines.
I can explain fuse, earthing, short circuit and overloading, and give three precautions.
I can calculate I = P/V for an appliance and choose a fuse rating.
I know the AC supply is 220 V, 50 Hz and reverses 100 times a second.
